questions.q: Without a feature store, why does a feature like "average rating over 7 days" tend to drift between training and serving?
options: Because it is computed by two different pieces of code, written at different times, that are supposed to agree but aren't kept in sync
Because Python cannot compute rolling averages
Because feature stores are required by law in most countries
Because training data is always synthetic
questions.explain: The core problem is two independently maintained code paths — a batch training-time query and a live serving-time function — that are meant to compute the same value but drift apart over time.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why isn't a shared table of pre-computed feature values enough by itself to prevent skew?
options: Shared tables are always too slow to query
If separate logic still populates that table for training versus serving, there are still two code paths that can drift, even though the storage is shared
Shared tables cannot be used by more than one model
Feast refuses to work with any shared table
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes between shared storage and a shared definition — storing values in one place doesn't help if two different pieces of logic populate that table differently for training and serving.

questions.q: In the Feast FeatureView example, what does the `entities=[driver]` argument specify?
options: The cloud region where the feature store runs
The join key the features are keyed on — here, driver_id
The machine learning algorithm to use
The password for accessing the online store
questions.explain: The `entities` argument ties the FeatureView to its join key (driver_id in this example), which is how Feast knows what each row's features belong to.

questions.q: What does it mean that a feature store is "a governance tool, not just a performance tool"?
options: It only affects how fast queries run
Centralized, reusable feature definitions make features discoverable, so new models reuse existing definitions and bug fixes benefit every model using them
It replaces the need for a legal compliance team
It has no effect on code reuse
questions.explain: Beyond latency, a feature store's governance value is reuse and discoverability: a fix or improvement to one definition benefits every model that uses it, instead of being patched into separate copies.

questions.q: What two things does a feature store deliver from a single feature definition?
options: A dashboard and an alerting rule
A way to compute historical values for training, and a way to serve the latest value fast for live prediction
A Docker image and a Kubernetes manifest
A SQL database and a REST API, unrelated to feature values
questions.explain: A feature store's defining capability is producing both a historical (training) path and a low-latency (serving) path from one single feature definition.
